free_tier.stated: The answer to the ten-minute-checkpoint question, computed from published inputs rather than measured. Take a checkpoint interval of 10 minutes, so the expected work lost per preemption is 5 minutes. With a preemption rate of 2.3 per cent an hour, the overhead is 0.19 per cent and the effective A100 80 GiB rate is USD 0.680 an hour. At 4.1 per cent an hour the overhead is 0.34 per cent and the rate is USD 0.681. Even at AWS's reported 17.5 per cent an hour for p4d, the overhead is 1.46 per cent, which raises USD 5.7337 to USD 5.8173. Survival of a one-hour run is 97.7 per cent at 2.3 per cent an hour, 96.0 per cent at 4.1 per cent, and 83.9 per cent at 17.5 per cent; over ten hours the same three are 79.5, 66.4 and 17.4 per cent.

chaining: This closes the loop between the discount and the checkpoint: a 10-minute checkpoint turns a 5.41 times discount into a 5.40 times discount, so the interruption risk costs almost nothing and the rate is the whole finding.
limits_note: Checkpointing every ten minutes makes preemption overhead a rounding error on every lane measured, so the discount is real rather than eaten by restarts; what breaks a run is the absence of a resume path, not the interruption rate.

notes: No provider publishes a run-survival figure. Azure publishes a per-hour eviction probability per SKU and region through Resource Graph over 28 trailing days, and GCP publishes a preemption rate through advice.capacityHistory, but neither is a survival curve and the two are not the same statistic: GCP divides preempted VMs by VMs that stopped running, which counts user-caused stops in the denominator and so understates the rate a long job experiences. GCP also publishes an estimated uptime in three buckets only (60 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 minute) from advice.capacity, which is the closest thing to a published survival figure and is coarse. The numbers above use third-party rates as the probability input, so the finding is inferred, not measured. The probe that would settle it: rent one A100 spot in eastus for 24 hours, checkpoint every 10 minutes to object storage, log every eviction with its timestamp and the scheduled-event offset, and repeat across 4 regions; that yields both the real per-hour rate and the real notice-to-eviction interval. qualifies-with-caveat via a05-spot; fails-identity via a05-spot; qualifies-with-caveat via a05-spot. The one recorded is the better-evidenced.
